Compacton equations and integrability: the Rosenau-Hyman and Cooper-Shepard-Sodano equations

R Hernández Heredero Affiliation:  Departamento de Matemática Aplicada a las TICUniversidad Politécnica de Madrid. C. Nikola Tesla s/n. 28031 Madrid. Spain    M Euler Affiliation:  Division of Mathematics, Department of Engineering Sciences and MathematicsLuleå University of Technology, SE-971 87 Luleå, Sweden    N Euler Affiliation:  Division of Mathematics, Department of Engineering Sciences and MathematicsLuleå University of Technology, SE-971 87 Luleå, Sweden    E G Reyes Affiliation:  Departamento de Matemática y Ciencia de la ComputaciónUniversidad de Santiago de Chile, Casilla 307 Correo 2, Santiago, Chile
April 2, 2019
Abstract

We study integrability –in the sense of admitting recursion operators– of two nonlinear equations which are known to possess compacton solutions: the K⁡(m,n)K(m,n) equation introduced by Rosenau and Hyman

Dt​(u)+Dx​(um)+Dx3​(un)=0,D_{t}(u)+D_{x}(u^{m})+D_{x}^{3}(u^{n})=0\;,

and the C​S​SCSS equation introduced by Coooper, Shepard, and Sodano,

Dt​(u)+ul−2​Dx​(u)+α​p​Dx​(up−1​ux2)+2​α​Dx2​(up​ux)=0.D_{t}(u)+u^{l-2}D_{x}(u)+\alpha pD_{x}(u^{p-1}u_{x}^{2})+2\alpha D_{x}^{2}(u^{p}u_{x})=0\;.

We obtain a full classification of integrable K⁡(m,n)K(m,n) and C​S​SCSS equations; we present their recursion operators, and we prove that all of them are related (via nonlocal transformations) to the Korteweg-de Vries equation. As an application, we construct isochronous hierarchies of equations associated to the integrable cases of C​S​SCSS. ††footnotetext: Mathematics Subject Classification: 37K05, 37K10, 35B10.††footnotetext: Keywords: Compacton, Rossenau-Hyman equation, Cooper-Shepard-Sodano equation, isochronous equation, formal integrability, recursion operator.

1 Introduction

We begin by quoting Rosenau [30]: ‘’We define a compact wave as a robust solitary wave with compact support beyond which it vanishes identically. We then define a compacton as a compact wave that preserves its shape after interacting with other compacton”. Rosenau and Hyman found examples of compactons while studying generalizations of the Korteweg-de Vries equation for which the dispersion term is nonlinear. Their model equation is the so-called K⁡(m,n)K(m,n) equation

ut+(um)x+(un)x​x​x=0,u_{t}+(u^{m})_{x}+(u^{n})_{xxx}=0\>, (1.1)

and an example of a compacton bearing equation within the family (1.1) is K⁡(2,2)K(2,2). In this case, the function u⁡(x,t)=(4​c/3)​cos2⁡((x−c​t)/4)u(x,t)=(4c/3)\cos^{2}((x-ct)/4) for |x−c​t|≤2​π|x-ct|\leq 2\pi and u⁡(x,t)=0u(x,t)=0 otherwise, is a compacton solution. Further works on compactons are [21, 22] and the comprehensive review [27].

It turns out that solutions to equations within the K⁡(m,n)K(m,n) can exhibit very complex behaviors; we refer the reader to [2, 3, 4], and to the papers [22, 27, 36] authored by Rosenau and his coworkers, for general discussions. Here, we just mention one example: in [31] the authors present four local conservation laws of K⁡(2,2)K(2,2), and credit P.J. Olver with the observation that no further local conservation laws seem to exist** * This observation has been proven rigorously by Vodová in 2013, see [35].. This (non)existence of conservation laws has an important analytic implication, see [36]: initially nonnegative, smooth and compactly supported solutions to K⁡(m,n)K(m,n) lose their smoothness within a finite time.

We wonder if this complex behavior has to do with (lack of) integrability. In this work we present a detailed study of the integrability properties of K⁡(m,n)K(m,n). We find that, module a rather general space of allowable transformations, the only integrable equations belonging to the K⁡(m,n)K(m,n) family are the KdV and modified KdV equations, and that integrable equations within the K⁡(m,n)K(m,n) family cannot have compacton solutions. In particular, we recover the observation in [18, 35] that K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) is not integrable.

In order to obtain this result we classify all integrable K⁡(m,n)K(m,n) equations using the theory of formal symmetries (to be summarized in Section 2). The power of this approach has been amply demonstrated by the classification results for evolution equations and systems of equations due to researchers such as Shabat, Fokas, Svinolupov, Sokolov, Mikhailov and others (see [24, 15, 32, 19, 16, 17]), and also by the important papers [33, 34] on the classification of integrable scalar evolution equations satisfying an homogeneity condition.

Since our search for integrable compacton bearing equations within the K⁡(m,n)K(m,n) class does not yield examples, we also investigate a related family, the Cooper-Shepard-Sodano family of equations

ut+ul−2​ux−α​p​Dx​(up−1​ux2)+2​α​Dx2​(up​ux)=0,α≠0,u_{t}+u^{l-2}u_{x}-\alpha pD_{x}\left(u^{p-1}u_{x}^{2}\right)+2\alpha D_{x}^{2}\left(u^{p}u_{x}\right)=0,\qquad\alpha\neq 0\;, (1.2)

introduced in [12]. We quote from this paper: “These equations have the same terms as the equations considered by Rosenau and Hyman, but the relative weights of the terms are quite different leading to the possibility that the integrability properties might be different”. The authors of [12] then proceed to show that their family of equations indeed admits compacton bearing equations. One such equation is (1.2) with l=3l=3, p=2p=2. This family of equations is further studied in [20, 14].

Encouraging properties of (1.2) are the facts that it admits a Hamiltonian formulation, and that it possesses three physically interesting conservation laws: area, mass and energy. Regretfully, we prove herein that they are not integrable in general. Using formal symmetries once more, we obtain six integrable equations within the (1.2) family. None of them can support compacton solutions.

Since the existence of compacton solutions is a rather extraordinary occurrence in the nonlinear world, we believe that our results are not only important by themselves, but also because they seem to express certain rigidity in our present algebraic/geometric/analytic approach to integrability. In other words, K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) say, must be “special”, and so far we have not been able to uncover the deeper source of its special character.

Our paper is organized as follows. We review the theory of formal symmetries and integrability in Section 2 after, essentially, [24], and in Section 3 we use this theory to classify integrable K⁡(m,n)K(m,n) equations. We note that a previous classification has appeared in [18]. One integrable case was missing therein and we single it out here. Fortunately, the missing case does not alter the conclusion in [18] that the only K⁡(m,n)K(m,n) integrable case are (essentially, module a class of allowable transformations specified in Section 3) the KdV and mKdV equations. The present classification also differs from the one appearing in [18] in that here we explain in detail how to connect our integrable cases to KdV (or, to the linear equation) and because in Section 5 we exhibit explicit recursion operators for all our integrable K⁡(m,n)K(m,n) equations. In Section 4 we study integrability of the Cooper-Shepard-Sodano family and again we are able to explain how to connect its integrable cases to KdV (or, to the linear equation), and to exhibit recursion operators. Finally in Section 6 we present an application of our results: we construct integrable isochronous equations, after [9, 10, 11], starting from the equations in our classification of integrable CSS equations, explain how to obtain their point symmetries, and present their corresponding recursion operators.

2 Formal symmetries and integrability

The formal symmetry approach to integrability [24, 25] begins with the observation that standard (systems of) partial differential equations which are integrable (for instance, in the sense of Calogero, see [8]) usually admit an infinite set of (generalized) symmetries of arbitrarily large differential order. A.B. Shabat and his collaborators, see for instance [24, 25], realized that it is possible to weaken the notion of a (generalized) symmetry to the notion of a formal symmetry —to be defined precisely below— and that this new concept provides a computationally efficient tool for defining integrability and classifying integrable equations. We recall from [24, 26] that G=(Gα)G=(G^{\alpha}) is a symmetry of a system of partial differential equations of the form Δa​(xi,uα,uxiα,…)=0\Delta_{a}(x^{i},u^{\alpha},u^{\alpha}_{x^{i}},\dots)=0, if

Δ∗​(G)=0\Delta_{*}(G)=0\; (2.1)

whenever uα​(xi)u^{\alpha}(x^{i}) is a solution to Δa=0\Delta_{a}=0, where Δ∗\Delta_{*} is the formal linearization of the system Δa=0\Delta_{a}=0, that is, Δ∗=(∑L∂Δa∂uLα​DL)\Delta_{*}=\left(\sum_{L}\frac{\partial\Delta_{a}}{\partial u_{L}^{\alpha}}D_{L}\right). If the system Δa=0\Delta_{a}=0 consists of just one scalar evolution equation,

Δ=ut−F,\Delta=u_{t}-F\;, (2.2)

then equation (2.1) becomes Dt​G=F∗​(G)D_{t}G=F_{*}(G) or, equivalently,

Dt​G=Dτ​F,D_{t}G=D_{\tau}F\;, (2.3)

where

Dτ=∑#​K≥0DK​(G)​∂∂uK.{D}_{\tau}=\sum_{\#K\geq 0}{D}_{K}(G)\,\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u_{K}}\;.

Note: Here and henceforth we use standard notation from the geometric theory of differential equations as presented in [26], see also [24].

Following [24, 25], we apply a second linearization to formula (2.3). We obtain, using some formulae appearing in [24],

(DtG)∗=(DτF)∗⇔Dt(G∗)+G∗∘F∗=Dτ(F∗)+F∗∘G∗,(D_{t}G)_{*}=(D_{\tau}F)_{*}\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad D_{t}(G_{*})+G_{*}\circ F_{*}=D_{\tau}(F_{*})+F_{*}\circ G_{*}\;, (2.4)

in which Dt​(∑LaL​DL)=∑LDt​(aL)​DLD_{t}(\sum_{L}a_{L}D_{L})=\sum_{L}D_{t}(a_{L})D_{L} if G∗=∑LaL​DLG_{\ast}=\sum_{L}a_{L}D_{L}, and the last equality holding on solutions to (2.2). The expression Dτ​(F∗)D_{\tau}(F_{*}) is defined analogously. We interpret our symmetry condition (2.4) using commutators:

Dt​(G∗)−[F∗,G∗]=Dτ​(F∗).D_{t}(G_{*})-[F_{*},G_{*}]=D_{\tau}(F_{*})\;. (2.5)

Let us consider the degree of the operators appearing in (2.5). The degree of F∗F_{*} as a differential operator —let us denote it by deg⁡(F∗)\deg(F_{*})— is the differential order of FF, i.e. the order of the differential equation (2.2) and thus, it is fixed. The degree of the left hand side of (2.5) depends on GG: Dt​(G∗)−[F∗,G∗]D_{t}(G_{*})-[F_{*},G_{*}] is a differential operator generically of degree deg⁡(G∗CLOSE\deg(G_{*}) plus deg⁡(F∗)\deg(F_{*}) minus 1, much higher than that of the operator in the right hand side, of degree deg⁡(F∗)\deg(F_{*}), if there are high order symmetries GG. Thus, it is not clear at all that non-trivial solutions to (2.5) should exist: the existence of (generalized) symmetries GG of arbitrarily high differential order must impose extremely strong constraints on the function FF.

Following [24, 25], and partially motivated by the theory of recursion operators, see [26], we define formal symmetries using the left hand side of Equation (2.5):

Definition 1.

Let ut=Fu_{t}=F be an evolution equation with FF a function of two independent variables xx, tt, one dependent variable uu and a finite number of derivatives of uu with respect to xx. A formal symmetry of rank kk of this partial differential equation is a formal pseudo-differential operator

Λ=lr​Dr+lr−1​Dr−1+⋯+l0+l−1​D−1+l−2​D−2+⋯,D=Dx\Lambda=l_{r}D^{r}+l_{r-1}D^{r-1}+\cdots+l_{0}+l_{-1}D^{-1}+l_{-2}D^{-2}+\cdots,\qquad D=D_{x} (2.6)

with lil_{i} being functions of tt, xx, uu and finite numbers of xx-derivatives of uu, that satisfies the equation

Dt​(Λ)=[F∗,Λ]D_{t}(\Lambda)=[F_{*},\Lambda] (2.7)

whenever uu is a solution to ut=Fu_{t}=F, up to a pseudo-differential operator of degree r+deg⁡(F∗)−kr+\deg(F_{*})-k. A formal symmetry of infinite rank is a pseudo-differential operator (2.6) such that (2.7) holds identically whenever uu is a solution to ut=Fu_{t}=F.

Note that if GG is a symmetry of order pp of ut=Fu_{t}=F, then (2.5) implies that G∗G_{*} is a formal symmetry of rank pp. We also remark that a formal symmetry of infinite rank is a recursion operator, see [26]. Thus, it generates, in principle, an infinite number of generalized symmetries of the equation at hand. For example, see [13], it can be proven that application of a quasilocal recursion operator (in the sense of [13, Section 1]) to a given symmetry yields a (generalized) symmetry, and so such an operator could indeed generate an infinite chain of (generalized) symmetries.

The main technical point behind Definition 1 is that the space of solutions of equation (2.7) is much richer and structured than that of equation (2.5) or even (2.1). For example, powers and roots of formal symmetries (computed using the standard theory of formal pseudo-differential operators, see [24, 26]) are also formal symmetries. In fact, this observation was one of the original motivations for the use of formal pseudo-differential operators in Definition 1, because the rrth root of a differential operator (2.6) is usually a pseudo-differential operator.

Now we explain why Definition 1 restricts the function FF. A theorem due to M. Adler, see [1], states that the residue (the coefficient of D−1D^{-1}) of a commutator of formal pseudo-differential operators is always a total derivative. If we apply this result to different powers Λi/r\Lambda^{i/r} of a generic formal symmetry †† † The foregoing discussion implies that instead of a general formal symmetry Λ\Lambda of degree rr, we can consider its rrth root Λ1/r\Lambda^{1/r} of degree 1 without loss of generality, see [24] for details. Λ\Lambda of rank kk inserted into (2.7), we obtain

Dt​(residue⁡(Λi/r))=residue⁡Dt​(Λi/r)=residue⁡[F∗,Λi/r]=D​σiD_{t}(\operatorname{residue}(\Lambda^{i/r}))=\operatorname{residue}{D_{t}(\Lambda^{i/r})}=\operatorname{residue}[F_{*},\Lambda^{i/r}]=D\sigma_{i}

for some differential functions σi\sigma_{i}, i.e. a sequence of conservation laws

Dtρi≐Dxσi,i=−1,1,…,D_{t}\rho_{i}\doteq D_{x}\sigma_{i},\qquad i=-1,1,\ldots, (2.8)

which are, together with the special case Dt​ρ0=Dt​(lr/lr−1)=Dx​σ0D_{t}\rho_{0}=D_{t}(l_{r}/l_{r-1})=D_{x}\sigma_{0}, the so called canonical conservation laws. The symbol ≐\doteq means that equations (2.8) must hold on solutions of (2.2), i.e. all derivatives with respect to tt must be substituted using the equation and its differential consequences.

As observed in [24], the canonical densities ρi\rho_{i} and conserved fluxes σi\sigma_{i} are differential functions which can be recursively written in terms of the right hand side FF of the equation and its derivatives. The fact that the left hand side of (2.8) must be a total derivative with respect to xx for all i=−1,1,2⋯i=-1,1,2\cdots, produces obstructions that are necessary conditions for the existence of (generalized/formal) symmetries GG, i.e. for integrability.

For example, for evolution equations of third order,

ut=F⁡(x,u,ux,ux​x,ux​x​x),u_{t}=F(x,u,u_{x},u_{xx},u_{xxx})\;, (2.9)

the first canonical density is ρ−1=(∂F/∂ux​x​x)−1/3\rho_{-1}=\left(\partial F\big/\partial u_{xxx}\right)^{-1/3}, see [24]. Therefore, a first integrability condition is requiring Dt​ρ−1D_{t}\rho_{-1} to be the total derivative of a local function σ−1\sigma_{-1}. The second canonical density imposes further differential restrictions on FF, and so forth. Usually, after a small number of steps our family of equations either fails to satisfy the integrability conditions, or the right hand side FF becomes so specific that we are able to produce a formal symmetry of infinite rank and therefore, in principle, a sequence of generalized symmetries of ut=Fu_{t}=F. If ut=Fu_{t}=F represents a family of equations, this procedure allows us to find all integrable cases in the family. We are led to the following precise definition of integrability, after [24, 26]:

Definition 2.

A system of evolution equations is integrable if and only if it possesses a formal symmetry of infinite rank.

Let us we write down the first five canonical densities for a third order equation (2.9) following [24]. We will use them in the next section to study the integrability of the Rosenau-Hyman and Cooper-Shepard-Sodano equations:

Proposition 1.

Let ut=F⁡(x,u,ux,ux​x,ux​x​x)u_{t}=F(x,u,u_{x},u_{xx},u_{xxx}) be an arbitrary third order evolution equation. The first five canonical conserved densities can be written explicitly as

ρ0\displaystyle\rho_{0} =ρ−13​∂F∂ux​x,\displaystyle=\rho_{-1}^{3}\frac{\partial F}{\partial u_{xx}}, (2.11)

Remark 1.

The condition of existence of a formal symmetry of infinite rank is strictly weaker than the condition of existence of an infinite number of generalized symmetries. Indeed, the 22 component system

{ut=ux​x​x​x+v2vt=vx​x​x​x,\left\{{\begin{array}[]{rl}u_{t}=&u_{xxxx}+v^{2}\\ v_{t}=&v_{xxxx}\;,\end{array}}\right.

considered by Bakirov in [5], possesses exactly one generalized symmetry, as proved by Beukers, Sanders and Wang [6]. On the other hand, it does possess a recursion operator [7].

Now, a very important remark, see [24] and also [26], is that the use of transformations between equations is a very convenient way to proceed when seeking classifications. In this paper we deal with integrable equations of the type

ut=f⁡(u)​ux​x​x+g⁡(u,ux,ux​x),u_{t}=f(u)u_{xxx}+g(u,u_{x},u_{xx})\;, (2.15)

see [31, 12]. The general strategy we use to classify these equations consists in performing a sequence of convenient point transformations and differential substitutions that preserve integrability, and then apply and compute the integrability conditions associated to (2.10)–(2.14). Our general procedure is as follows:

First, if f′​(u)≠0f^{\prime}(u)\neq 0 the point transformation u→f(u)−1/3u\to f(u)^{-1/3} converts Equation (2.15) into another one of the form

ut=Dx​[ux​xu3+f1​(u,ux)]+f2​(u,ux,ux​x),u_{t}=D_{x}\left[\frac{u_{xx}}{u^{3}}+f_{1}(u,u_{x})\right]+f_{2}(u,u_{x},u_{xx})\;, (2.16)

where f2​(u,ux,ux​x)f_{2}(u,u_{x},u_{xx}) is not a total xx-derivative. This form is very convenient because it follows from (2.10) that the integrability condition Dt​ρ−1=Dx​σ−1D_{t}\rho_{-1}=D_{x}\sigma_{-1} is equivalent to requiring that f2=0f_{2}=0. This condition greatly restricts the form of the equation. Once f2=0f_{2}=0, the equation admits a potentiation u→uxu\to u_{x} that brings it into the form ut=ux​x​x/ux3+f1​(ux,ux​x)u_{t}=u_{xxx}/u_{x}^{3}+f_{1}(u_{x},u_{xx}). A subsequent hodograph transformation x→ux\to u, u→xu\to x simplifies it to one of the form

ut=ux​x​x+h⁡(ux,ux​x).u_{t}=u_{xxx}+h(u_{x},u_{xx}).

This equation can be “antipotentiated” (ux→uu_{x}\to u) to get

ut=ux​x​x+Dx​h​(u,ux).u_{t}=u_{xxx}+D_{x}h(u,u_{x}).

Our integrability conditions imply that the integrable cases of this equation are all of the form

ut=ux​x​x+Dx​[h2​(u)​ux2+(a+b​u)​ux+h0​(u)].u_{t}=u_{xxx}+D_{x}\left[h_{2}(u)u_{x}^{2}+\left(a+bu\right)u_{x}+h_{0}(u)\right]. (2.17)

If h2​(u)≠0h_{2}(u)\neq 0 a further point transformation ∫exp⁡[23​∫h2​(u)​𝑑u]​𝑑u→u\int\!\exp\left[\frac{2}{3}\int\!{h_{2}(u)\,du}\right]\,du\to u transforms this equation into another one of the form

ut=ux​x​x+(a+b​u)​ux​x+f1​(u)​ux3+f2​(u)​ux2+f3​(u)​ux.u_{t}=u_{xxx}+(a+bu)\,u_{xx}+f_{1}(u)\,u_{x}^{3}+f_{2}(u)\,u_{x}^{2}+f_{3}(u)\,u_{x}. (2.18)

We will show that all the integrable cases of the RH and CSS equations can be written in the form (2.18), as linear equations, KdV or mKdV, or the Calogero-Degasperis-Fokas (CDF) equation (see below; the CDF is Miura-transformable to KdV). Thus, if we “pullback” the recursion operator of KdV (or, the linear equation) by the foregoing transformations, we can construct recursion operators of the original equations, and therefore we obtain an explicit proof of integrability in terms of Definition 2. In actual fact, we seldom perform this pullback operation explicitly. Once we know that a given equation is integrable, it is usually straightforward to compute its recursion operator from first principles, as in [29].

Now we carry out this plan.

3 Integrability of the Rosenau-Hyman equation

We consider the compacton equation of Rosenau and Hyman (see [31])

Dt​(u)+Dx​(um)+Dx3​(un)=0,n≠0.D_{t}(u)+D_{x}(u^{m})+D_{x}^{3}(u^{n})=0,\qquad n\neq 0\;. (3.1)

As we informed in Section 2, DtD_{t} and DxD_{x} are total derivatives with respect to independent variables tt and xx. For simplicity, we use the subindex notation ut=Dt​uu_{t}=D_{t}u, ux=Dx​uu_{x}=D_{x}u, ux​x=Dx2u_{xx}=D_{x}^{2} but we prefer to use the total derivative notation when applied to a more complicated differential function, e.g. Dx​(um)=m​um−1​uxD_{x}(u^{m})=mu^{m-1}u_{x}.

The case n=1n=1 i.e.

ut+m​um−1​ux+ux​x​x=0,u_{t}+mu^{m-1}u_{x}+u_{xxx}=0\;,

is well-known, see [24, Section 4.1]: the only integrable cases are m=0,1,2,3m=0,1,2,3, i.e. the linear equation, the KdV and the modified KdV equations. We write them as (using the point transformation x→−xx\to-x)

ut\displaystyle u_{t} =ux​x​x+α​ux+β,α,β∈𝐂,\displaystyle=u_{xxx}+\alpha\,u_{x}+\beta,\quad\alpha,\beta\in\mathbf{C}, (3.2)
ut\displaystyle u_{t} =ux​x​x+2​u​ux,\displaystyle=u_{xxx}+2\,uu_{x}, (3.3)
ut\displaystyle u_{t} =ux​x​x+3​u2​ux.\displaystyle=u_{xxx}+3\,u^{2}u_{x}. (3.4)

If n≠1n\neq 1, the point transformation x→−xx\to-x, t→t/nt\to t/n, u→u3/(1−n)u\to u^{3/(1-n)} changes (3.1) into equations of the form (2.16), namely:

ut=Dx​[ux​xu3−m⁡(n−1)n⁡(3​m−n−2)​u2−3​m+n−1+n−9​n2​(n−1)​ux2u4]+(n+2)​(2​n+1)​ux3(n−1)2​u5u_{t}=D_{x}\left[\frac{u_{xx}}{u^{3}}-\frac{m(n-1)}{n(3m-n-2)}u^{\frac{2-3m+n}{-1+n}}-\frac{9n}{2(n-1)}\frac{u_{x}^{2}}{u^{4}}\right]+\frac{(n+2)(2n+1)u_{x}^{3}}{(n-1)^{2}u^{5}} (3.5)

if 3​m−n−2≠03m-n-2\neq 0, and

ut=Dx​[ux​xu3−9​n2​(n−1)​ux2u4+(n+2)3​n​log⁡u]+(n+2)​(2​n+1)​ux3(n−1)2​u5u_{t}=D_{x}\left[\frac{u_{xx}}{u^{3}}-\frac{9n}{2(n-1)}\frac{u_{x}^{2}}{u^{4}}+\frac{(n+2)}{3n}\log{u}\right]+\frac{(n+2)(2n+1)u_{x}^{3}}{(n-1)^{2}u^{5}} (3.6)

if 3​m−n−2=03m-n-2=0.

The first integrability condition Dt​ρ−1=Dx​σ−1D_{t}\rho_{-1}=D_{x}\sigma_{-1} or, equivalently, ut∈Im⁡Dxu_{t}\in\operatorname{Im}D_{x} implies that either n=−2n=-2 or n=−1/2n=-1/2 in both cases, because the last term in (3.5) and (3.6) must be zero. The composition of a potentiation, a hodograph and an antipotentiation yields the following equations of the form (2.17):

ut=ux​x​x+Dx​[32​n+2n−1​ux2u+m⁡(n−1)n⁡(3​m−n−2)​u3​(m−1)n−1],u_{t}=u_{xxx}+D_{x}\left[\frac{3}{2}\frac{n+2}{n-1}\frac{u_{x}^{2}}{u}+\frac{m(n-1)}{n(3m-n-2)}\,u^{\frac{3(m-1)}{n-1}}\right], (3.7)
ut=ux​x​x+Dx​[32​(n+2n−1)​ux2u+n+23​n​u​log⁡u].u_{t}=u_{xxx}+D_{x}\left[\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{n+2}{n-1}\right)\frac{u_{x}^{2}}{u}+\frac{n+2}{3n}\,u\log{u}\right]. (3.8)

If n=−2n=-2, Equation (3.7) becomes

ut=ux​x​x−m−12​u−m​uxu_{t}=u_{xxx}-\frac{m-1}{2}u^{-m}u_{x}

whose integrable cases are again m=1,0,−1,−2m=1,0,-1,-2, corresponding to linear equations, KdV and mKdV. On the other hand, if n=−2n=-2, Equation (3.8) becomes a linear equation included in case (3.2).

If n=−1/2n=-1/2, Equation (3.7) can be written in the form (2.18), this is,

ut=ux​x​x−12​ux3−4​m​(m−1)2​m−1​e(1−2​m)​u​ux,u_{t}=u_{xxx}-\frac{1}{2}u_{x}^{3}-\frac{4m(m-1)}{2m-1}\,{\rm e}^{(1-2m)u}u_{x}\;,

after a point transformation u→euu\to{\rm e}^{u}. This family of equations satisfies the first two integrability conditions. The third integrability condition is Dt​ρ1∈Im⁡DxD_{t}\rho_{1}\in\operatorname{Im}D_{x}, and the canonical conserved density ρ1\rho_{1} satisfies

Dt​(ρ1)∼−2​(m−1)​m​(2​m−3)​(2​m+1)​eu−2​m​u​ux3,D_{t}(\rho_{1})\sim-2(m-1)m(2m-3)(2m+1)e^{u-2mu}u_{x}^{3}\;,

in which the symbol ∼\sim denotes equality except for the addition of a total xx-derivative. Thus, integrability can be achieved only in the cases m=−1/2m=-1/2, 00, 11, 3/23/2‡‡ ‡ We note that the case n=−1/2n=-1/2, m=3/2m=3/2 was missing in [18]. which are all subcases of the Calogero-Degasperis-Fokas (CDF) equation

ut=ux​x​x−12​ux3+(α​e2​u+β​e−2​u+γ)​ux.u_{t}=u_{xxx}-\frac{1}{2}u_{x}^{3}+\left(\alpha{\rm e}^{2u}+\beta{\rm e}^{-2u}+\gamma\right)u_{x}\;. (3.9)

Finally, when n=−1/2n=-1/2 Equation (3.8) becomes

ut=ux​x​x−3​ux​ux​xu+32​ux3u2−(1+log⁡u)​uxu_{t}=u_{xxx}-3\frac{u_{x}u_{xx}}{u}+\frac{3}{2}\frac{u_{x}^{3}}{u^{2}}-(1+\log{u})u_{x}

and for it

Dt​(ρ1)∼−2​ux3u3D_{t}(\rho_{1})\sim-2\frac{u_{x}^{3}}{u^{3}}

so this case is not integrable.

Remark 2.

We note that the CDF equation (3.9) can be related to the KdV equation through the Miura transformation

32​ux​x−34​ux2−6​β​e−u​ux−12​α​e2​u−12​β​e−2​u−γ2→u.\frac{3}{2}u_{xx}-\frac{3}{4}u_{x}^{2}-\sqrt{6\beta}{\rm e}^{-u}u_{x}-\frac{1}{2}\alpha e^{2u}-\frac{1}{2}\beta e^{-2u}-\frac{\gamma}{2}\to u\;.

We summarize the integrable cases of the Rosenau-Hyman family (3.1) in the following theorem. We make the point transformation x→−xx\to-x, t→t/nt\to t/n and write

ut=1n​Dx​(um)+1n​Dx3​(un),n≠0u_{t}=\tfrac{1}{n}D_{x}(u^{m})+\tfrac{1}{n}D_{x}^{3}(u^{n})\;,\qquad n\neq 0 (3.10)

instead of (3.1). This transformation is invertible and does not affect integrability.

Theorem 1.

The integrable cases of the Rosenau-Hyman family (3.10) are

  1. 1.

    n=1n=1, m=0,1,2,3m=0,1,2,3, corresponding to Equations (3.2), (3.3) and (3.4), namely,

    ut\displaystyle u_{t} =ux​x​x+α​ux+β,α,β∈𝐂,\displaystyle=u_{xxx}+\alpha\,u_{x}+\beta,\quad\alpha,\beta\in\mathbf{C}, (3.11)
    ut\displaystyle u_{t} =ux​x​x+2​u​ux,\displaystyle=u_{xxx}+2\,uu_{x}, (3.12)
    ut\displaystyle u_{t} =ux​x​x+3​u2​ux.\displaystyle=u_{xxx}+3\,u^{2}u_{x}\;. (3.13)
  2. 2.

    n=−2n=-2, m=−2,−1,0,1m=-2,-1,0,1, corresponding to Equations

    ut\displaystyle u_{t} =Dx​[Dx​(uxu3)−12​u2],\displaystyle=D_{x}\left[D_{x}\left(\frac{u_{x}}{u^{3}}\right)-\frac{1}{2u^{2}}\right]\;, (3.14)
    ut\displaystyle u_{t} =Dx​[Dx​(uxu3)−12​u],\displaystyle=D_{x}\left[D_{x}\left(\frac{u_{x}}{u^{3}}\right)-\frac{1}{2u}\right]\;, (3.15)
    ut\displaystyle u_{t} =−12​Dx3​[u−2],\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}D_{x}^{3}\left[u^{-2}\right]\;, (3.16)
    ut\displaystyle u_{t} =Dx​[Dx​(uxu3)−12​u]\displaystyle=D_{x}\left[D_{x}\left(\frac{u_{x}}{u^{3}}\right)-\frac{1}{2}u\right] (3.17)

    respectively.

  3. 3.

    n=−12n=-\tfrac{1}{2}, m=32,1,0,−12m=\tfrac{3}{2},1,0,-\tfrac{1}{2}, corresponding to Equations

    ut\displaystyle u_{t} =Dx​[Dx​(uxu3/2)−2​u3/2],\displaystyle=D_{x}\left[D_{x}\left(\frac{u_{x}}{u^{3/2}}\right)-2u^{3/2}\right], (3.18)
    ut\displaystyle u_{t} =Dx​[Dx​(uxu3/2)−2​u],\displaystyle=D_{x}\left[D_{x}\left(\frac{u_{x}}{u^{3/2}}\right)-2u\right], (3.19)
    ut\displaystyle u_{t} =Dx2​[uxu3/2],\displaystyle=D_{x}^{2}\left[\frac{u_{x}}{u^{3/2}}\right], (3.20)
    ut\displaystyle u_{t} =Dx​[Dx​(uxu3/2)−2​1u1/2]\displaystyle=D_{x}\left[D_{x}\left(\frac{u_{x}}{u^{3/2}}\right)-2\frac{1}{u^{1/2}}\right]\; (3.21)

    respectively.

All these equations are related to the linear equation or to the KdV equation through differential substitutions.

Remark 3.

It is clear that the equations appearing above cannot admit solutions with compact support, let alone compactons. As explained in Section 1, this theorem extends and enriches the discussion on K⁡(m,n)K(m,n) appearing in [18]. We mention that J. Vodová classified conservation laws of the K⁡(m,m)K(m,m) equations and observed that K⁡(−2,−2)K(-2,-2), K(−1/2,−1/2)K(-1/2,-1/2) are integrable; integrability of K⁡(−2,−2)K(-2,-2), K(−1/2,−1/2)K(-1/2,-1/2), and K⁡(−1,−2)K(-1,-2), is also observed in the later review [27].

4 Integrability of Cooper-Shepard-Sodano

In this section we study equations of the form

ut+ul−2​ux−α​p​Dx​(up−1​ux2)+2​α​Dx2​(up​ux)=0,α≠0.u_{t}+u^{l-2}u_{x}-\alpha pD_{x}\left(u^{p-1}u_{x}^{2}\right)+2\alpha D_{x}^{2}\left(u^{p}u_{x}\right)=0,\qquad\alpha\neq 0. (4.1)

We consider the case p=0p=0 first. Equation (4.1) becomes ut+ul−2​ux+2​α​ux​x​x=0u_{t}+u^{l-2}u_{x}+2\alpha u_{xxx}=0, which is integrable if and only if l=2,3,4l=2,3,4, i.e. in the linear, KdV and mKdV case, as observed in [24]. Let us now consider p≠0p\neq 0. We use the same strategy as with the Rosenau-Hyman case: first we apply the change t→−tt\to-t, u→(2αu3)−1/pu\to(2\alpha u^{3})^{-1/p} to obtain

ut=Dx​[ux​xu3−3​(2​p+3)2​p​ux2u4−p​(2​α)2−lp3​l−p−6​u6−3​l+pp]+(p+3)​(p+6)​ux32​p2​u5u_{t}=D_{x}\left[\frac{u_{xx}}{u^{3}}-\frac{3(2p+3)}{2p}\frac{u_{x}^{2}}{u^{4}}-\frac{p(2\alpha)^{\frac{2-l}{p}}}{3l-p-6}u^{\frac{6-3l+p}{p}}\right]+\frac{(p+3)(p+6)u_{x}^{3}}{2p^{2}u^{5}} (4.2)

if 3​l−p−6≠03l-p-6\neq 0, and

ut=Dx​[ux​xu3−3​(2​p+3)2​p​ux2u4+12​α3​log⁡u]+(p+3)​(p+6)​ux32​p2​u5u_{t}=D_{x}\left[\frac{u_{xx}}{u^{3}}-\frac{3(2p+3)}{2p}\frac{u_{x}^{2}}{u^{4}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{2\alpha}}\log{u}\right]+\frac{(p+3)(p+6)u_{x}^{3}}{2p^{2}u^{5}} (4.3)

if 3​l−p−6=03l-p-6=0.

Thus, the first integrability condition of Proposition 1 fixes the values p=−3p=-3 or p=−6p=-6. If p=−3p=-3, a combination of potentiation, hodograph, antipotentiation and exponential point transformation u→euu\to{\rm e}^{u} , with a scaling to absorb the constant α\alpha, change (4.2) and (4.3) into the equations

ut=ux​x​x−ux32+(l−2)​eu−l​u​uxl−1 and ut=ux​x​x−ux32+u​uxu_{t}=u_{xxx}-\frac{u_{x}^{3}}{2}+\frac{(l-2)e^{u-lu}u_{x}}{l-1}\quad\text{ and }\quad u_{t}=u_{xxx}-\frac{u_{x}^{3}}{2}+uu_{x}\;

respectively. On the other hand, if p=−6p=-6, the same combination of transformations, using u→u2u\to u^{2} instead of the exponential, changes (4.2) and (4.3) into

ut=ux​x​x+(l−2)l​uxul and ut=ux​x​x+log⁡(u)​uxu_{t}=u_{xxx}+\frac{(l-2)}{l}\frac{u_{x}}{u^{l}}\quad\text{ and }\quad u_{t}=u_{xxx}+\log(u)u_{x}\;

respectively.

Let us assume that 3​l−p−6≠03l-p-6\neq 0. The integrability condition in ρ1\rho_{1} implies that if p=−3p=-3 we must have l=−1,2,3l=-1,2,3, and if p=−6p=-6, then l=−2,−1,2l=-2,-1,2 and we recover again the linear, KdV, mKdV and CDF equations. When 3​l−p−6=03l-p-6=0, we have the CSS equations

ut=au6​ux​x​x−12​au7​ux​ux​x+21​au8​ux3+uxu2u_{t}=\frac{a}{u^{6}}u_{xxx}-12\frac{a}{u^{7}}u_{x}u_{xx}+21\frac{a}{u^{8}}u_{x}^{3}+\frac{u_{x}}{u^{2}}

(p=−6p=-6 and l=0l=0) and

ut=au3​ux​x​x−6​au4​ux​ux​x+6​au5​ux3+uxu,u_{t}=\frac{a}{u^{3}}u_{xxx}-6\frac{a}{u^{4}}u_{x}u_{xx}+6\frac{a}{u^{5}}u_{x}^{3}+\frac{u_{x}}{u}\;,

(p=−3p=-3 and l=1l=1), in which a=2​αa=2\alpha. The integrability condition for ρ2\rho_{2} implies that both equations are not integrable.

Summarizing, we have the following theorem.

Theorem 2.

The integrable equations of family (4.1) are

  1. 1.

    p=0,p=0, l=2,3,4l=2,3,4, corresponding to the linear equation, KdV equation, mKdV equation;

  2. 2.

    p=−6p=-6, l=−2,−1,2l=-2,-1,2, corresponding to the Equations

    ut=au6​ux​x​x−12​au7​ux​ux​x+21​au8​ux3+uxu4,\displaystyle u_{t}=\frac{a}{u^{6}}u_{xxx}-12\frac{a}{u^{7}}u_{x}u_{xx}+21\frac{a}{u^{8}}u_{x}^{3}+\frac{u_{x}}{u^{4}}, (4.4)
    ut=au6​ux​x​x−12​au7​ux​ux​x+21​au8​ux3+uxu3,\displaystyle u_{t}=\frac{a}{u^{6}}u_{xxx}-12\frac{a}{u^{7}}u_{x}u_{xx}+21\frac{a}{u^{8}}u_{x}^{3}+\frac{u_{x}}{u^{3}}, (4.5)
    ut=au6​ux​x​x−12​au7​ux​ux​x+21​au8​ux3+ux.\displaystyle u_{t}=\frac{a}{u^{6}}u_{xxx}-12\frac{a}{u^{7}}u_{x}u_{xx}+21\frac{a}{u^{8}}u_{x}^{3}+u_{x}. (4.6)

    respectively.

  3. 3.

    p=−3,p=-3, l=−1,2,3l=-1,2,3, corresponding to the Equations

    ut=au3​ux​x​x−6​au4​ux​ux​x+6​au5​ux3+uxu3,\displaystyle u_{t}=\frac{a}{u^{3}}u_{xxx}-6\frac{a}{u^{4}}u_{x}u_{xx}+6\frac{a}{u^{5}}u_{x}^{3}+\frac{u_{x}}{u^{3}}, (4.7)
    ut=au3​ux​x​x−6​au4​ux​ux​x+6​au5​ux3+ux,\displaystyle u_{t}=\frac{a}{u^{3}}u_{xxx}-6\frac{a}{u^{4}}u_{x}u_{xx}+6\frac{a}{u^{5}}u_{x}^{3}+u_{x}, (4.8)
    ut=au3​ux​x​x−6​au4​ux​ux​x+6​au5​ux3+u​ux.\displaystyle u_{t}=\frac{a}{u^{3}}u_{xxx}-6\frac{a}{u^{4}}u_{x}u_{xx}+6\frac{a}{u^{5}}u_{x}^{3}+uu_{x}. (4.9)

    respectively.

All these equations are related to the linear equation or to the KdV equation through differential substitutions.

As in Section 3, this theorem implies that no integrable CSS equation admits solutions with compact support.

R1​[u]∘ux=0.R_{1}[u]\circ u_{x}=0.


On the other hand, Equations (4.7), (4.8) and (4.9) are special cases of Equation (85) in [29], namely

ut=a​ux​x​xu3−6​a​ux​ux​xu4+6​a​ux3u5+β1​uxu3+β2​u​ux+β3​ux,u_{t}=\frac{au_{xxx}}{u^{3}}-6\frac{au_{x}u_{xx}}{u^{4}}+6\frac{au_{x}^{3}}{u^{5}}+\beta_{1}\frac{u_{x}}{u^{3}}+\beta_{2}uu_{x}+\beta_{3}u_{x}, (5.9)

where aa, β1\beta_{1}, β2\beta_{2} and β3\beta_{3} are arbitrary constants and a≠0a\neq 0. This equation admits the following recursion operator:

R2​[u]=1u2​Dx2−3​uxu3​Dx−3​ux​xu3+6​ux2u4+β23​a​u2+β1a​1u2−1autDx−1∘1+4​β23​auxDx−1∘u+β3auxDx−1∘1.R_{2}[u]=\frac{1}{u^{2}}D_{x}^{2}-\frac{3u_{x}}{u^{3}}D_{x}-3\frac{u_{xx}}{u^{3}}+6\frac{u_{x}^{2}}{u^{4}}+\frac{\beta_{2}}{3a}u^{2}+\frac{\beta_{1}}{a}\frac{1}{u^{2}}\\[5.69046pt] -\frac{1}{a}u_{t}\,D_{x}^{-1}\circ 1+\frac{4\beta_{2}}{3a}u_{x}\,D_{x}^{-1}\circ u+\frac{\beta_{3}}{a}u_{x}\,D_{x}^{-1}\circ 1. (5.10)

Acting R2​[u]R_{2}[u] on the tt-translation symmetry ut​∂∂u\displaystyle{u_{t}\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u}}, we obtain a symmetry-integrable hierarchy of order 2​m+32m+3, namely

ut=R2m​[u]∘(a​ux​x​xu3−6​a​ux​ux​xu4+6​a​ux3u5+β1​uxu3+β2​u​ux+β3​ux),\displaystyle u_{t}=R_{2}^{m}[u]\circ\left(\frac{au_{xxx}}{u^{3}}-6\frac{au_{x}u_{xx}}{u^{4}}+6\frac{au_{x}^{3}}{u^{5}}+\beta_{1}\frac{u_{x}}{u^{3}}+\beta_{2}uu_{x}+\beta_{3}u_{x}\right), (5.11)
m=0,1,2,…,\displaystyle m=0,1,2,\ldots\;,

and we note that for the xx-translation symmetry we obtain

R2​[u]∘ux=0.R_{2}[u]\circ u_{x}=0.

6 The isochronous equations for (5.6) and (5.9)

In this section we construct new integrable evolution equations starting from what we will call the Cooper-Shepard-Sodano model equations (5.6) and (5.9). Our new equations are isochronous in the sense of Calogero, see [9, Chapter 7] and [23, 10, 11]: they are autonomous evolution PDEs which depend on a positive parameter ω\omega and possess many solutions which are time-periodic with period T=2​π/ωT=2\pi/\omega. For completeness, we also explain how to obtain the Lie point symmetries of our equations and present their recursion operators.

6.1 Isochronous equations

Following [23, 10, 9, 11], we introduce a new dependent variable v⁡(r,s)v(r,s), where rr and ss are new independent variables, as follows:

u⁡(x,t)=e−i​λ​ω​s​v​(r,s)\displaystyle u(x,t)=e^{-i\lambda\omega s}v(r,s) (6.1a)
x=r​ei​μ​ω​s\displaystyle x=re^{i\mu\omega s} (6.1b)
t=1i​ω​(ei​ω​s−1).\displaystyle t=\frac{1}{i\omega}\left(e^{i\omega s}-1\right). (6.1c)

The prolongations are

ut=e−i⁡(λ+1)​ω​s​[vs−i​λ​ω​v−i​μ​ω​r​vr]\displaystyle u_{t}=e^{-i(\lambda+1)\omega s}\left[v_{s}-i\lambda\omega\,v-i\mu\omega r\,v_{r}\right]
un​x=e−i⁡(λ+n​μ)​ω​svn​r,n=1,2,3,…,\displaystyle u_{nx}=e^{-i(\lambda+n\mu)\omega s}\,v_{nr},\quad n=1,2,3,\dots,

where

un​x=∂nu∂xn,vn​r=∂nv∂rn.u_{nx}=\frac{\partial^{n}u}{\partial x^{n}},\qquad v_{nr}=\frac{\partial^{n}v}{\partial r^{n}}.

With the change of variables (6.1a) – (6.1c), equation (5.6) takes the form

vs−i​λ​ω​v−i​μ​ω​r​vr=ei⁡(6​λ−3​μ+1)​ω​s​(a​vr​r​rv6−12​a​vr​vr​rv7+21​a​vr3v8)+β1​ei⁡(4​λ−μ+1)​ω​s​(vrv4)+β2​ei⁡(3​λ−μ+1)​ω​s​(vrv3)+β3​ei⁡(−μ+1)​ω​s​vr.v_{s}-i\lambda\omega v-i\mu\omega rv_{r}=e^{i(6\lambda-3\mu+1)\omega s}\left(\frac{av_{rrr}}{v^{6}}-\frac{12av_{r}v_{rr}}{v^{7}}+\frac{21av_{r}^{3}}{v^{8}}\right)\\[5.69046pt] \qquad+\beta_{1}e^{i(4\lambda-\mu+1)\omega s}\,\left(\frac{v_{r}}{v^{4}}\right)+\beta_{2}e^{i(3\lambda-\mu+1)\omega s}\,\left(\frac{v_{r}}{v^{3}}\right)+\beta_{3}e^{i(-\mu+1)\omega s}\,v_{r}. (6.3)

This equation can become autonomous for a≠0a\neq 0 only if

μ=2​λ+13,\mu=2\lambda+\frac{1}{3},

so that (6.3) then takes the form

vs−i​λ​ω​v−i⁡(2​λ+13)​ω​r​vr=a​vr​r​rv6−12​a​vr​vr​rv7+21​a​vr3v8+β1​ei⁡(2​λ+23)​ω​s​(vrv4)+β2​ei⁡(λ+23)​ω​s​(vrv3)+β3​ei⁡(2​λ+23)​ω​s​vr.v_{s}-i\lambda\omega v-i\left(2\lambda+\frac{1}{3}\right)\omega rv_{r}=\frac{av_{rrr}}{v^{6}}-\frac{12av_{r}v_{rr}}{v^{7}}+\frac{21av_{r}^{3}}{v^{8}}\\[5.69046pt] +\beta_{1}e^{i(2\lambda+\frac{2}{3})\omega s}\,\left(\frac{v_{r}}{v^{4}}\right)+\beta_{2}e^{i(\lambda+\frac{2}{3})\omega s}\,\left(\frac{v_{r}}{v^{3}}\right)+\beta_{3}e^{i(2\lambda+\frac{2}{3})\omega s}\,v_{r}. (6.4)

Clearly (6.4), and therefore (6.3), becomes autonomous in the following three cases:
Case 1.1: λ=−13\displaystyle{\lambda=-\frac{1}{3}} and μ=−13\displaystyle{\mu=-\frac{1}{3}} with β2=β3=0\beta_{2}=\beta_{3}=0. Then (6.3) becomes

vs+i​13​ω​v+i​13​ω​r​vr=a​vr​r​rv6−12​a​vr​vr​rv7+21​a​vr3v8+β1​vrv4.v_{s}+i\frac{1}{3}\omega v+i\frac{1}{3}\omega rv_{r}=\frac{av_{rrr}}{v^{6}}-\frac{12av_{r}v_{rr}}{v^{7}}+\frac{21av_{r}^{3}}{v^{8}}+\beta_{1}\frac{v_{r}}{v^{4}}. (6.5)

Case 1.2: λ=−23\displaystyle{\lambda=-\frac{2}{3}} and μ=−1\displaystyle{\mu=-1} with β1=β3=0\beta_{1}=\beta_{3}=0. Then (6.3) becomes

vs+i​23​ω​v+i​ω​r​vr=a​vr​r​rv6−12​a​vr​vr​rv7+21​a​vr3v8+β2​vrv3.v_{s}+i\frac{2}{3}\omega v+i\omega rv_{r}=\frac{av_{rrr}}{v^{6}}-\frac{12av_{r}v_{rr}}{v^{7}}+\frac{21av_{r}^{3}}{v^{8}}+\beta_{2}\frac{v_{r}}{v^{3}}. (6.6)

Case 1.3: λ=13\displaystyle{\lambda=\frac{1}{3}} and μ=1\displaystyle{\mu=1} with β1=β2=0\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=0. Then (6.3) becomes

vs−i​13​ω​v−i​ω​r​vr=a​vr​r​rv6−12​a​vr​vr​rv7+21​a​vr3v8+β3​vr.v_{s}-i\frac{1}{3}\omega v-i\omega rv_{r}=\frac{av_{rrr}}{v^{6}}-\frac{12av_{r}v_{rr}}{v^{7}}+\frac{21av_{r}^{3}}{v^{8}}+\beta_{3}v_{r}. (6.7)


Now we consider (5.9). With the change of variables (6.1a) – (6.1c), Equation (5.9) takes the form

vs−i​λ​ω​v−i​μ​ω​r​vr=ei⁡(3​λ−3​μ+1)​ω​s​(a​vr​r​rv3−6​a​vr​vr​rv4+6​a​vr3v5)+β1​ei⁡(3​λ−μ+1)​ω​s​(vrv3)+β2​ei⁡(−λ−μ+1)​ω​s​v​vr+β3​ei⁡(−μ+1)​ω​s​vr.v_{s}-i\lambda\omega v-i\mu\omega rv_{r}=e^{i(3\lambda-3\mu+1)\omega s}\left(\frac{av_{rrr}}{v^{3}}-\frac{6av_{r}v_{rr}}{v^{4}}+\frac{6av_{r}^{3}}{v^{5}}\right)\\[5.69046pt] \qquad+\beta_{1}e^{i(3\lambda-\mu+1)\omega s}\,\left(\frac{v_{r}}{v^{3}}\right)+\beta_{2}e^{i(-\lambda-\mu+1)\omega s}\,vv_{r}+\beta_{3}e^{i(-\mu+1)\omega s}\,v_{r}. (6.8)

This equation can become autonomous for a≠0a\neq 0 only if

μ=λ+13,\mu=\lambda+\frac{1}{3},

so that (6.8) then takes the form

vs−i​λ​ω​v−i⁡(λ+13)​ω​r​vr=a​vr​r​rv3−6​a​vr​vr​rv4+6​a​vr3v5+β1​ei⁡(2​λ+23)​ω​s​(vrv3)+β2​ei⁡(−2​λ+23)​ω​s​v​vr+β3​ei⁡(−λ+23)​ω​s​vr.v_{s}-i\lambda\omega v-i\left(\lambda+\frac{1}{3}\right)\omega rv_{r}=\frac{av_{rrr}}{v^{3}}-\frac{6av_{r}v_{rr}}{v^{4}}+\frac{6av_{r}^{3}}{v^{5}}\\[5.69046pt] \qquad+\beta_{1}e^{i(2\lambda+\frac{2}{3})\omega s}\,\left(\frac{v_{r}}{v^{3}}\right)+\beta_{2}e^{i(-2\lambda+\frac{2}{3})\omega s}\,vv_{r}+\beta_{3}e^{i(-\lambda+\frac{2}{3})\omega s}\,v_{r}. (6.9)

Clearly (6.9), and therefore (6.8), becomes autonomous in the following three cases:

Case 2.1: λ=−13\displaystyle{\lambda=-\frac{1}{3}} and μ=0\displaystyle{\mu=0} with β2=β3=0\beta_{2}=\beta_{3}=0. Then (6.8) becomes

vs+i​13​ω​v=a​vr​r​rv3−6​a​vr​vr​rv4+6​a​vr3v5+β1​vrv3.v_{s}+i\frac{1}{3}\omega v=\frac{av_{rrr}}{v^{3}}-\frac{6av_{r}v_{rr}}{v^{4}}+\frac{6av_{r}^{3}}{v^{5}}+\beta_{1}\,\frac{v_{r}}{v^{3}}. (6.10)

Case 2.2: λ=13\displaystyle{\lambda=\frac{1}{3}} and μ=23\displaystyle{\mu=\frac{2}{3}} with β1=β3=0\beta_{1}=\beta_{3}=0. Then (6.8) becomes

vs−i​13​ω​v−i​23​ω​r​vr=a​vr​r​rv3−6​a​vr​vr​rv4+6​a​vr3v5+β2​v​vr.v_{s}-i\frac{1}{3}\omega v-i\frac{2}{3}\omega rv_{r}=\frac{av_{rrr}}{v^{3}}-\frac{6av_{r}v_{rr}}{v^{4}}+\frac{6av_{r}^{3}}{v^{5}}+\beta_{2}\,vv_{r}. (6.11)

Case 2.3: λ=23\displaystyle{\lambda=\frac{2}{3}} and μ=1\displaystyle{\mu=1} with β1=β2=0\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=0. Then (6.8) becomes

vs−i​23​ω​v−i​ω​r​vr=a​vr​r​rv3−6​a​vr​vr​rv4+6​a​vr3v5+β3​vr.v_{s}-i\frac{2}{3}\omega v-i\omega rv_{r}=\frac{av_{rrr}}{v^{3}}-\frac{6av_{r}v_{rr}}{v^{4}}+\frac{6av_{r}^{3}}{v^{5}}+\beta_{3}\,v_{r}. (6.12)

Our isochronous equations are (6.5)–(6.7) and (6.10)–(6.12).

6.2 Symmetries

We list the Lie point symmetries of equation (5.6), that is

ut=a​ux​x​xu6−12​a​ux​ux​xu7+21​a​ux3u8+β1​uxu4+β2​uxu3+β3​ux.u_{t}=\frac{au_{xxx}}{u^{6}}-12\frac{au_{x}u_{xx}}{u^{7}}+21\frac{au_{x}^{3}}{u^{8}}+\beta_{1}\frac{u_{x}}{u^{4}}+\beta_{2}\frac{u_{x}}{u^{3}}+\beta_{3}u_{x}.

Besides the obvious xx-translation, Zx=∂∂x\displaystyle{Z_{x}=\frac{\partial\ }{\partial x}}, and tt-translation symmetry, Zt=∂∂t\displaystyle{Z_{t}=\frac{\partial\ }{\partial t}}, Equation (5.6) also admits the following point symmetries:

  • a)

    For β1=β2=β3=0\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=\beta_{3}=0:

    Z1=x​∂∂x+3​t​∂∂t,Z2=u​∂∂u+6​t​∂∂t.Z_{1}=x\frac{\partial\ }{\partial x}+3t\frac{\partial\ }{\partial t},\quad Z_{2}=u\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u}+6t\frac{\partial\ }{\partial t}.
  • b)

    For β1=β2=0\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=0 and β3≠0\beta_{3}\neq 0:

    Z1=(x−2​t​β3)​∂∂x+3​t​∂∂t,Z2=u​∂∂u+6​t​∂∂t−6​t​β3​∂∂x.Z_{1}=(x-2t\beta_{3})\frac{\partial\ }{\partial x}+3t\frac{\partial\ }{\partial t},\quad Z_{2}=u\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u}+6t\frac{\partial\ }{\partial t}-6t\beta_{3}\frac{\partial\ }{\partial x}.
  • c)

    For β1=β3=0\beta_{1}=\beta_{3}=0 and β2≠0\beta_{2}\neq 0:

    Z1=−23​u​∂∂u+x​∂∂x−t​∂∂t.Z_{1}=-\frac{2}{3}u\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u}+x\frac{\partial\ }{\partial x}-t\frac{\partial\ }{\partial t}.
  • d)

    For β2=β3=0\beta_{2}=\beta_{3}=0 and β1≠0\beta_{1}\neq 0:

    Z1=−u​∂∂u+x​∂∂x−3​t​∂∂t.Z_{1}=-u\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u}+x\frac{\partial\ }{\partial x}-3t\frac{\partial\ }{\partial t}.


We list the Lie point symmetries of equation (5.9), that is

ut=a​ux​x​xu3−6​a​ux​ux​xu4+6​a​ux3u5+β1​uxu3+β2​u​ux+β3​ux.u_{t}=\frac{au_{xxx}}{u^{3}}-6\frac{au_{x}u_{xx}}{u^{4}}+6\frac{au_{x}^{3}}{u^{5}}+\beta_{1}\frac{u_{x}}{u^{3}}+\beta_{2}uu_{x}+\beta_{3}u_{x}.

Besides the obvious xx-translation symmetry and tt-translation symmetry, (5.9) also admits the following point symmetries:

  • a)

    For β1=β2=β3=0\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=\beta_{3}=0:

    Z1=x​∂∂x+3​t​∂∂t,Z2=u​∂∂u+3​t​∂∂t,Z3=x​u​∂∂u−12​x2​∂∂x.Z_{1}=x\frac{\partial\ }{\partial x}+3t\frac{\partial\ }{\partial t},\quad Z_{2}=u\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u}+3t\frac{\partial\ }{\partial t},\quad Z_{3}=xu\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u}-\frac{1}{2}x^{2}\frac{\partial\ }{\partial x}.
  • b)

    For β1=β2=0\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=0 and β3≠0\beta_{3}\neq 0:

    Z1=(x−2​t​β3)​∂∂x+3​t​∂∂t,Z2=u​∂∂u+3​t​∂∂t−3​t​β3​∂∂x\displaystyle Z_{1}=(x-2t\beta_{3})\frac{\partial\ }{\partial x}+3t\frac{\partial\ }{\partial t},\quad Z_{2}=u\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u}+3t\frac{\partial\ }{\partial t}-3t\beta_{3}\frac{\partial\ }{\partial x}
    Z3=u⁡(x+β3​t)​∂∂u−12​(x+β3​t)2​∂∂x.\displaystyle Z_{3}=u(x+\beta_{3}t)\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u}-\frac{1}{2}(x+\beta_{3}t)^{2}\frac{\partial\ }{\partial x}.
  • c)

    For β1=β3=0\beta_{1}=\beta_{3}=0 and β2≠0\beta_{2}\neq 0:

    Z1=u​∂∂u−2​x​∂∂x−3​t​∂∂t.Z_{1}=u\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u}-2x\frac{\partial\ }{\partial x}-3t\frac{\partial\ }{\partial t}.
  • d)

    For β2=β3=0\beta_{2}=\beta_{3}=0 and β1≠0\beta_{1}\neq 0:

    Z1=u​∂∂u+3​t​∂∂t\displaystyle Z_{1}=u\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u}+3t\frac{\partial\ }{\partial t}
    Z2=usin(a−1/2β11/2x)∂∂u+a1/2β1−1/2cos(a−1/2β11/2x)∂∂x\displaystyle Z_{2}=u\sin\left(a^{-1/2}\beta_{1}^{1/2}x\right)\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u}+a^{1/2}\beta_{1}^{-1/2}\cos\left(a^{-1/2}\beta_{1}^{1/2}x\right)\frac{\partial\ }{\partial x}
    Z3=ucos(a−1/2β11/2x)∂∂u−a1/2β1−1/2sin(a−1/2β11/2x)∂∂x.\displaystyle Z_{3}=u\cos\left(a^{-1/2}\beta_{1}^{1/2}x\right)\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u}-a^{1/2}\beta_{1}^{-1/2}\sin\left(a^{-1/2}\beta_{1}^{1/2}x\right)\frac{\partial\ }{\partial x}.

We can now obviously map the symmetries of (5.6) and (5.9) with the (6.1a) – (6.1c) to symmetries of the isochronous equations (6.3) and (6.8). For example, in vertical form the xx-translation symmetry

ux​∂∂u,u_{x}\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u},

then takes the form

e−i​μ​ω​s​vr​∂∂v,e^{-i\mu\omega s}v_{r}\frac{\partial\ }{\partial v},

for (6.3) and (6.8), whereas the tt-translation symmetry

ut​∂∂u,u_{t}\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u},

becomes the symmetry

e−i​ω​s​(vs−i​λ​ω​v−i​μ​ω​r​vr)​∂∂ve^{-i\omega s}\left(v_{s}-i\lambda\omega v-i\mu\omega rv_{r}\right)\frac{\partial\ }{\partial v}

for (6.3) and (6.8).

6.3 The isochronous hierarchies for (5.6) and (5.9)

For equation (5.6) we have the hierarchy (5.8), namely

ut=R1m[u]∘(a​ux​x​xu6−12a​ux​ux​xu7+21a​ux3u8+β1uxu4+β2uxu3+β3ux,)\displaystyle u_{t}=R_{1}^{m}[u]\circ\left(\frac{au_{xxx}}{u^{6}}-12\frac{au_{x}u_{xx}}{u^{7}}+21\frac{au_{x}^{3}}{u^{8}}+\beta_{1}\frac{u_{x}}{u^{4}}+\beta_{2}\frac{u_{x}}{u^{3}}+\beta_{3}u_{x},\right)
m=0,1,2,…,\displaystyle m=0,1,2,\ldots\ ,

where R1​[u]R_{1}[u] is given by (5.7). Corresponding to the above Case 1.1, Case 1.2 and Case 1.3, the isochronous hierarchies are the following:

Case 1.1: We consider the hierarchy (5.8) with β2=β3=0\beta_{2}=\beta_{3}=0. This leads to the following isochronous hierarchy

vs+i⁡(12​m+3)​ω​v+i⁡(12​m+3)​ω​r​vr=Rm11[v]∘(a​vr​r​rv6−12​a​vr​vr​rv7+21​a​vr3v8+β1vrv4),m=0,1,2,…,v_{s}+i\left(\frac{1}{2m+3}\right)\omega v+i\left(\frac{1}{2m+3}\right)\omega rv_{r}\\ \qquad=R^{m}_{11}[v]\circ\left(\frac{av_{rrr}}{v^{6}}-\frac{12av_{r}v_{rr}}{v^{7}}+\frac{21av_{r}^{3}}{v^{8}}+\beta_{1}\frac{v_{r}}{v^{4}}\right),\quad m=0,1,2,\ldots\ , (6.13)

where

R11​[v]=1v4​Dr2−6​vrv5​Dr−6​vr​rv5+22​vr2v6+4​β13​a​1v2−2a(a​vr​r​rv6−12​a​vr​vr​rv7+21​a​vr3v8+β1vrv4)Dr−1∘v+vrDr−1∘(−2​vr​rv6+6vr2v7+2​β13​a1v3).R_{11}[v]=\frac{1}{v^{4}}D_{r}^{2}-\frac{6v_{r}}{v^{5}}D_{r}-\frac{6v_{rr}}{v^{5}}+\frac{22v_{r}^{2}}{v^{6}}+\frac{4\beta_{1}}{3a}\frac{1}{v^{2}}\\ \qquad-\frac{2}{a}\left(\frac{av_{rrr}}{v^{6}}-\frac{12av_{r}v_{rr}}{v^{7}}+\frac{21av_{r}^{3}}{v^{8}}+\beta_{1}\frac{v_{r}}{v^{4}}\right)D_{r}^{-1}\circ v\\ \qquad+v_{r}D_{r}^{-1}\circ\left(-\frac{2v_{rr}}{v^{6}}+6\frac{v_{r}^{2}}{v^{7}}+\frac{2\beta_{1}}{3a}\frac{1}{v^{3}}\right).

The first member of the hierarchy (6.13) for m=0m=0 is the equation (6.5).

Case 1.2: We consider the hierarchy (5.8) with β1=β3=0\beta_{1}=\beta_{3}=0. This leads to the following isochronous hierarchy

vs+i⁡(22​m+3)​ω​v+i⁡(32​m+3)​ω​r​vr=Rm12[v]∘(a​vr​r​rv6−12​a​vr​vr​rv7+21​a​vr3v8+β1vrv4),m=0,1,2,…,v_{s}+i\left(\frac{2}{2m+3}\right)\omega v+i\left(\frac{3}{2m+3}\right)\omega rv_{r}\\ \qquad=R^{m}_{12}[v]\circ\left(\frac{av_{rrr}}{v^{6}}-\frac{12av_{r}v_{rr}}{v^{7}}+\frac{21av_{r}^{3}}{v^{8}}+\beta_{1}\frac{v_{r}}{v^{4}}\right),\quad m=0,1,2,\ldots\ , (6.14)

where

R12​[v]=1v4​Dr2−6​vrv5​Dr−6​vr​rv5+22​vr2v6+2​β2a​1v−2a(a​vr​r​rv6−12​a​vr​vr​rv7+21​a​vr3v8+β2vrv3)Dr−1∘v+vrDr−1∘(−2​vr​rv6+6vr2v7+β2a1v2).R_{12}[v]=\frac{1}{v^{4}}D_{r}^{2}-\frac{6v_{r}}{v^{5}}D_{r}-\frac{6v_{rr}}{v^{5}}+\frac{22v_{r}^{2}}{v^{6}}+\frac{2\beta_{2}}{a}\frac{1}{v}\\ \qquad-\frac{2}{a}\left(\frac{av_{rrr}}{v^{6}}-\frac{12av_{r}v_{rr}}{v^{7}}+\frac{21av_{r}^{3}}{v^{8}}+\beta_{2}\frac{v_{r}}{v^{3}}\right)D_{r}^{-1}\circ v\\ \qquad+v_{r}D_{r}^{-1}\circ\left(-\frac{2v_{rr}}{v^{6}}+6\frac{v_{r}^{2}}{v^{7}}+\frac{\beta_{2}}{a}\frac{1}{v^{2}}\right).

The first member of the hierarchy (6.14) for m=0m=0 is the equation (6.6).

Case 1.3: We consider the hierarchy (5.8) with β1=β2=0\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=0. This leads to the following isochronous hierarchy

vs+i​λ​ω​v+i⁡(2​λ+12​m+3)​ω​r​vr=Rm13[v]∘(a​vr​r​rv6−12​a​vr​vr​rv7+21​a​vr3v8+β3vr),m=1,2,…v_{s}+i\lambda\omega v+i\left(2\lambda+\frac{1}{2m+3}\right)\omega rv_{r}\\ \qquad=R^{m}_{13}[v]\circ\left(\frac{av_{rrr}}{v^{6}}-\frac{12av_{r}v_{rr}}{v^{7}}+\frac{21av_{r}^{3}}{v^{8}}+\beta_{3}v_{r}\right),\quad m=1,2,\ldots (6.15)

where λ\lambda is arbitrary and
